    latex_statement: |-
      For the max statistic context, \(S_{n,j}\) is the \(j\)th coordinate of the sum
      \[
      S_n=\frac{1}{\sqrt n}\sum_{i=1}^n (X_i-\mathbb E[X_i]),
      \]
      involving i.i.d. vectors \(X_1,\dots,X_n\) in \(\mathbb R^p\). If we let
      \[
      \sigma_j^2=\operatorname{Var}(X_{1,j}) \quad \text{for each } 1\leq j\leq p,
      \]
      and write \(\sigma_{(1)}\geq \dots \geq \sigma_{(p)}\), these are the ordered standard deviations.

      If we let \(\tau_n\in [0,1]\) be a free parameter, then we can consider the partially standardized statistic
      \begin{equation}\label{eqn:mdef}
      M=\max_{1\leq j\leq p} S_{n,j}/\sigma_j^{\tau_n}.
      \end{equation}

      Let \(\tilde S_n\sim N(0,\Sigma)\) and define the Gaussian counterpart of the partially standardized statistic \(M\) (\ref{eqn:mdef}) according to
      \begin{equation}\label{eqn:Mtildedef}
      \tilde M=\max_{1\leq j\leq p} \tilde{S}_{n,j}/\sigma_j^{\tau_n}.
      \end{equation}

      Recall that for any random variables \(U\) and \(V\), the Kolmogorov distance is given by
      \[
      d_{\mathrm K}(\mathcal{L}(U),\mathcal{L}(V))=\sup_{t\in\mathbb R}|\mathbb P(U\leq t)-\mathbb P(V\leq t)|.
      \]

      To state the structural assumptions, for any \(d\in\{1,\dots,p\}\), let \(\J(d)\) denote a set of indices corresponding to the \(d\) largest values among \(\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_p\), i.e.,
      \[
      \{\sigma_{(1)},\dots,\sigma_{(d)}\}= \{\sigma_j| \ j\in\J(d)\}.
      \]
      In addition, let \(R(d)\in\mathbb R^{d\times d}\) denote the correlation matrix of the random variables
      \(\{X_{1,j}\,|\, j\in\J(d)\}\). Write \(R_{i,j}(d)\) for the \((i,j)\)-entry of \(R(d)\), and set \(R_{i,j}^+(d)=\max\{R_{i,j}(d),0\}\).

      Lastly, let \(a\in(0,\frac{1}{2})\) be a constant fixed with respect to \(n\), and define the integers \(\ell_n\) and \(k_n\) according to
      \begin{align}
      \ell_n&=\big\lceil (1\vee \log(n)^3)\wedge p\big\rceil\\[0.2cm]
      k_n&=\big\lceil \big(\ell_n\vee n^{\frac{1}{\log(n)^{a}}}\big)\wedge p\big\rceil.\label{eqn:kndef}
      \end{align}
      Note that both \(\ell_n\) and \(k_n\) grow slower than any fractional power of \(n\), and always satisfy \(1\leq \ell_n\leq k_n\leq p\).

      The symbol \(\lesssim\) is used in the usual asymptotic sense, with an implied constant not depending on \(n\).

      ### Definitions and notation used in Proof
      To fix some notation that will be used in the appendices, let \(d\in\{1,\dots,p\}\), and define a generalized version of \(M\) as
      \[
      M_d=\max_{j\in\J(d)}S_{n,j}/\sigma_j^{\tau_n}.
      \]
      In particular, the statistic \(M\) defined in equation~\eqref{eqn:mdef} is the same as \(M_p\). Similarly, the Gaussian version of \(M_d\) is defined as
      \[
      \tilde M_d=\max_{j\in\J(d)}\tilde S_{n,j}/\sigma_j^{\tau_n}.
      \]

      Based on the formulation of the theorems, it is sufficient to show that the results hold for all large values of \(n\), and it will simplify some of the proofs to make use of this reduction. For this reason, it is understood going forward that \(n\) is sufficiently large for any given expression to make sense. Another convention is that all proofs in the appendices will implicitly assume that \(p>k_n\) (unless otherwise stated), because once the proofs are given for this case, it will follow that the low-dimensional case where \(p\leq k_n\) can be handled as a direct consequence.

      ### Proof
      Consider the inequality
      \begin{equation}
      d_{\mathrm K}(\mathcal{L}(M_p),\mathcal{L}(\tilde M_p)) \, \leq \, I_n+II_n+III_n,
      \end{equation}
      where we define
      \begin{align}
      I_n &= d_{\mathrm K}\Big(\mathcal{L}(M_p) \, , \, \mathcal{L}(M_{k_n})\Big)\\[0.2cm]
      II_n &=d_{\mathrm K}\Big( \mathcal{L}(M_{k_n})\, , \, \mathcal{L}(\tilde M_{k_n})\Big)\\[0.2cm]
      III_n &=d_{\mathrm K}\Big( \mathcal{L}(\tilde M_{k_n})\, ,\, \mathcal{L}(\tilde M_p)\Big).\label{eqn:IIIdef}
      \end{align}

      Below, we show that the term \(II_n\) is at most of order \(n^{-\frac{1}{2}+\delta}\) in [ref:R1]. Later on, we establish a corresponding result for \(I_n\) and \(III_n\) in [ref:R2]. Taken together, these results complete the proof of Theorem~\ref{THM:G} for the case \(p>k_n\).

      In the low-dimensional case \(p\leq k_n\), the previous proofs relied on the condition \(p>k_n\) only insofar as this implies \(k_n\geq n^{\frac{1}{\log(n)^a}}\) and \(\ell_n\geq \log(n)^3\). However, if \(p\leq k_n\), then the definition of \(k_n\) implies that \(p=k_n\), which causes the quantities \(I_n\) and \(III_n\) to become exactly \(0\). In this case, the proof of Theorem~\ref{THM:G} reduces to bounding \(II_n\), and this argument can be repeated as before.

      ##### Proposition~\ref{prop:bentkus}: bound for \(\II_n\)
      ###### Definitions and notation
      For the max-statistic setting, \(S_{n,j}\) is the \(j\)th coordinate of
      \[
      S_n=\frac1{\sqrt n}\sum_{i=1}^n (X_i-\E[X_i]),
      \]
      where \(X_1,\dots,X_n\) are i.i.d. random vectors in \(\R^p\). Let
      \[
      \sigma_j^2=\var(X_{1,j}),\qquad 1\le j\le p,
      \]
      and write the ordered standard deviations as
      \[
      \sigma_{(1)}\ge \sigma_{(2)}\ge\cdots\ge \sigma_{(p)}.
      \]

      For a free parameter \(\tau_n\in[0,1]\), define
      \[
      M=\max_{1\le j\le p} \frac{S_{n,j}}{\sigma_j^{\tau_n}}
      \qquad\text{(source label \texttt{eqn:mdef}).}
      \]
      Let \(\tilde S_n\sim N(0,\Sigma)\), and define the Gaussian counterpart
      \[
      \tilde M=\max_{1\le j\le p}\frac{\tilde S_{n,j}}{\sigma_j^{\tau_n}}
      \qquad\text{(source label \texttt{eqn:Mtildedef}).}
      \]

      For random variables \(U,V\), the Kolmogorov distance is
      \[
      d_{\mathrm K}\big(\mathcal L(U),\mathcal L(V)\big)
      =\sup_{t\in\R}\big|\P(U\le t)-\P(V\le t)\big|.
      \]

      For each \(d\in\{1,\dots,p\}\), let \(J(d)\) denote a set of indices corresponding to the \(d\) largest values among \(\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_p\), i.e.
      \[
      \{\sigma_{(1)},\dots,\sigma_{(d)}\}=\{\sigma_j:j\in J(d)\}.
      \]
      Let \(R(d)\in\R^{d\times d}\) denote the correlation matrix of the random variables
      \[
      \{X_{1,j}:j\in J(d)\}.
      \]
      The entries of \(R(d)\) are written \(R_{i,j}(d)\), and \(R^+(d)\) denotes the matrix with \((i,j)\) entry
      \[
      R^+_{i,j}(d)=\max\{R_{i,j}(d),0\}.
      \]

      For \(d\in\{1,\dots,p\}\), define the generalized statistic
      \[
      M_d=\max_{j\in J(d)}\frac{S_{n,j}}{\sigma_j^{\tau_n}},
      \]
      so that \(M=M_p\). Similarly,
      \[
      \tilde M_d=\max_{j\in J(d)}\frac{\tilde S_{n,j}}{\sigma_j^{\tau_n}},
      \]
      so that \(\tilde M=\tilde M_p\). In particular, for the integer \(k_n\) defined below,
      \[
      M_{k_n}=\max_{j\in J(k_n)}\frac{S_{n,j}}{\sigma_j^{\tau_n}},
      \qquad
      \tilde M_{k_n}=\max_{j\in J(k_n)}\frac{\tilde S_{n,j}}{\sigma_j^{\tau_n}}.
      \]

      The quantity \(\II_n\) is defined by
      \[
      \II_n
      =d_{\mathrm K}\Big(\mathcal L(M_{k_n}),\mathcal L(\tilde M_{k_n})\Big).
      \]

      Let \(a\in(0,\frac12)\) be fixed with respect to \(n\), and define the integers
      \[
      \ell_n=\big\lceil (1\vee \log(n)^3)\wedge p\big\rceil,
      \]
      \[
      k_n=\Big\lceil \big(\ell_n\vee n^{\frac1{\log(n)^a}}\big)\wedge p\Big\rceil
      \qquad\text{(source label \texttt{eqn:kndef}).}
      \]
      The source notes that both \(\ell_n\) and \(k_n\) grow slower than any fractional power of \(n\), and always satisfy
      \[
      1\le \ell_n\le k_n\le p.
      \]

      The symbol \(\lesssim\) is used in the source’s usual asymptotic sense, with an implied constant not depending on \(n\).

      ###### Assumptions
      Fix \(\delta\in(0,\frac12)\).

      We consider a sequence of models indexed by \(n\), with all parameters depending on \(n\) except those stated to be fixed. In particular, \(p=p(n)\) is regarded as a function of \(n\); if a constant does not depend on \(n\), it does not depend on \(p\) either.

      **Assumption 2.1 (Data-generating model) [`A:model`].**

      (i) There is a vector \(\mu=\mu(n)\in\R^p\) and a positive semi-definite matrix \(\Sigma=\Sigma(n)\in\R^{p\times p}\) such that the observations \(X_1,\dots,X_n\in\R^p\) are generated as
      \[
      X_i=\mu+\Sigma^{1/2}Z_i,\qquad 1\le i\le n,
      \]
      where the random vectors \(Z_1,\dots,Z_n\in\R^p\) are i.i.d.

      (ii) The random vector \(Z_1\) satisfies
      \[
      \E[Z_1]=0,\qquad \E[Z_1Z_1^{\top}]=\mathbf I_p,
      \]
      and
      \[
      \sup_{\|u\|_2=1}\|Z_1^{\top}u\|_{\psi_1}\le c_0
      \]
      for some constant \(c_0>0\) that does not depend on \(n\), where \(\|\cdot\|_{\psi_1}\) is the sub-exponential Orlicz norm. No constraint is placed on the ratio \(p/n\).

      **Assumption 2.2 (Structural assumptions) [`A:cor`].**

      (i) The parameters \(\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_p\) are positive, and there are positive constants \(\alpha\), \(c\), and \(c_\circ\in(0,1)\), not depending on \(n\), such that
      \[
      \sigma_{(j)}\le c\,j^{-\alpha}\qquad\text{for all }j\in\{k_n,\dots,p\}
      \qquad\text{(source label \texttt{eqn:varcond1}),}
      \]
      and
      \[
      \sigma_{(j)}\ge c_\circ\,j^{-\alpha}\qquad\text{for all }j\in\{1,\dots,k_n\}
      \qquad\text{(source label \texttt{eqn:varcond2}).}
      \]

      (ii) There is a constant \(\varepsilon_0\in(0,1)\), not depending on \(n\), such that
      \[
      \max_{i\ne j}R_{i,j}(\ell_n)\le 1-\varepsilon_0
      \qquad\text{(source label \texttt{eqn:cormax}).}
      \]
      Also, the matrix \(R^+(\ell_n)\), with \((i,j)\) entry
      \[
      \max\{R_{i,j}(\ell_n),0\},
      \]
      is positive semi-definite, and there is a constant \(C>0\), not depending on \(n\), such that
      \[
      \sum_{1\le i<j\le \ell_n} R^+_{i,j}(\ell_n)\le C\ell_n
      \qquad\text{(source label \texttt{eqn:corbound}).}
      \]

      **Theorem~\ref{THM:G} condition on \(\tau_n\).** In addition,
      \[
      \tau_n\in[0,1)
      \qquad\text{and}\qquad
      (1-\tau_n)\sqrt{\log(n)}\gtrsim 1.
      \]

      The supplement’s asymptotic convention is that it suffices to prove the stated bound for all sufficiently large \(n\); this convention is used in the appendix.

      ###### Statement
      Fix any number \(\delta\in(0,\frac12)\), and suppose that the conditions of Theorem~\ref{THM:G} hold, as spelled out in Assumptions above. Then,
      \[
      \II_n\ \lesssim\ n^{-\frac12+\delta}
      \qquad\text{(source label \texttt{eqn:IInbound}).}
      \]

      ##### Proposition~\ref{prop:IandIII}

      ###### Definitions and notation
      Let \(X_1,\dots,X_n\) be i.i.d. vectors in \(\R^p\), and for the max statistic context let \(S_{n,j}\) be the \(j\)th coordinate of
      \[
      S_n=\frac{1}{\sqrt n}\sum_{i=1}^n (X_i-\E[X_i]).
      \]
      Let
      \[
      \sigma_j^2=\var(X_{1,j}) \qquad \text{for each }1\leq j\leq p,
      \]
      and write \(\sigma_{(1)}\geq \cdots \geq \sigma_{(p)}\) for the ordered standard deviations.

      Let \(\tau_n\in[0,1]\) be the free partial-standardization parameter, and define
      \begin{equation}\label{eqn:mdef}
      M=\max_{1\leq j\leq p} S_{n,j}/\sigma_j^{\tau_n}.
      \end{equation}
      Let \(\tilde S_n\sim N(0,\Sigma)\), and define the Gaussian counterpart
      \begin{equation}\label{eqn:Mtildedef}
      \tilde{M}=\max_{1\leq j\leq p} \tilde{S}_{n,j}/\sigma_j^{\tau_n}.
      \end{equation}
      For random variables \(U\) and \(V\), the Kolmogorov distance is
      \[
      d_{\textup K}(\mathcal{L}(U),\mathcal{L}(V))
      =\sup_{t\in\R}\left|\P(U\leq t)-\P(V\leq t)\right|.
      \]

      For any \(d\in\{1,\dots,p\}\), let \(\J(d)\) denote a set of indices corresponding to the \(d\) largest values among \(\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_p\), i.e.
      \[
      \{\sigma_{(1)},\dots,\sigma_{(d)}\}
      =
      \{\sigma_j:\ j\in\J(d)\}.
      \]
      Let \(R(d)\in\R^{d\times d}\) denote the correlation matrix of the random variables
      \[
      \{X_{1,j}:\ j\in\J(d)\}.
      \]

      Let \(a\in(0,\tfrac12)\) be a constant fixed with respect to \(n\), and define the integers \(\ell_n\) and \(k_n\) by
      \begin{align}
      \ell_n&=\big\lceil (1\vee \log(n)^3)\wedge p\big\rceil,\\[0.2cm]
      k_n&=\big\lceil \big(\ell_n\vee n^{\frac{1}{\log(n)^{a}}}\big)\wedge p\big\rceil
      \label{eqn:kndef}.
      \end{align}
      Both \(\ell_n\) and \(k_n\) grow slower than any fractional power of \(n\), and
      \[
      1\leq \ell_n\leq k_n\leq p.
      \]

      For \(d\in\{1,\dots,p\}\), define the generalized statistic
      \[
      M_d=\max_{j\in\J(d)}S_{n,j}/\sigma_j^{\tau_n},
      \]
      so that \(M=M_p\), and define its Gaussian analog
      \[
      \tilde M_d=\max_{j\in\J(d)}\tilde S_{n,j}/\sigma_j^{\tau_n}.
      \]
      The quantities appearing in the statement are
      \begin{align}
      \I_n &= d_{\textup K}\Big(\mathcal{L}(M_p),\mathcal{L}(M_{k_n})\Big),\\[0.2cm]
      \III_n &= d_{\textup K}\Big(\mathcal{L}(\tilde M_{k_n}),\mathcal{L}(\tilde M_p)\Big)
      \label{eqn:IIIdef}.
      \end{align}

      ###### Assumptions
      The result is stated for a sequence of models indexed by \(n\), with all parameters depending on \(n\) except those stated to be fixed. In particular, \(p=p(n)\) is regarded as a function of \(n\), and constants that do not depend on \(n\) do not depend on \(p\) either.

      Fix any number \(\delta\in(0,1/2)\). The proposition assumes that the conditions of Theorem~\ref{THM:G} hold. These conditions are as follows.

      **Assumption 2.1 (Data-generating model) [A:model]**

      (i) There is a vector \(\mu=\mu(n)\in\R^p\) and a positive semidefinite matrix \(\Sigma=\Sigma(n)\in\R^{p\times p}\), such that the observations \(X_1,\dots,X_n\in\R^p\) are generated as
      \[
      X_i=\mu+\Sigma^{1/2}Z_i
      \qquad\text{for each }1\leq i\leq n,
      \]
      where the random vectors \(Z_1,\dots,Z_n\in\R^p\) are i.i.d.

      (ii) The random vector \(Z_1\) satisfies
      \[
      \E[Z_1]=0,
      \qquad
      \E[Z_1Z_1^\top]=\mathbf{I}_p,
      \]
      and
      \[
      \sup_{\|u\|_2=1}\|Z_1^\top u\|_{\psi_1}\leq c_0,
      \]
      for some constant \(c_0>0\) that does not depend on \(n\). No constraint is placed on the ratio \(p/n\).

      **Assumption 2.2 (Structural assumptions) [A:cor]**

      (i) The parameters \(\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_p\) are positive, and there are positive constants \(\alpha\), \(c\), and \(c_{\circ}\in(0,1)\), not depending on \(n\), such that
      \begin{equation}\label{eqn:varcond1}
      \sigma_{(j)} \leq c\, j^{-\alpha}
      \qquad\text{for all }j\in\{k_n,\dots,p\},
      \end{equation}
      and
      \begin{equation}\label{eqn:varcond2}
      \sigma_{(j)} \geq c_{\circ}\, j^{-\alpha}
      \qquad\text{for all }j\in\{1,\dots,k_n\}.
      \end{equation}

      (ii) There is a constant \(\epsilon_0\in(0,1)\), not depending on \(n\), such that
      \begin{equation}\label{eqn:cormax}
      \max_{i\neq j}R_{i,j}(\ell_n)\leq 1-\epsilon_0.
      \end{equation}
      Also, the matrix \(R^+(\ell_n)\), with \((i,j)\) entry given by
      \[
      \max\{R_{i,j}(\ell_n),0\},
      \]
      is positive semidefinite, and there is a constant \(C>0\), not depending on \(n\), such that
      \begin{equation}\label{eqn:corbound}
      \sum_{1\leq i<j\leq \ell_n} R_{i,j}^+(\ell_n)\leq C\ell_n.
      \end{equation}

      In addition, \(\tau_n\in[0,1)\) and
      \[
      (1-\tau_n)\sqrt{\log(n)}\gtrsim 1.
      \]

      The appendix’s general convention says that proofs implicitly assume \(p>k_n\) unless otherwise stated. The source separately notes that when \(p\leq k_n\), one has \(p=k_n\), so that \(\I_n\) and \(\III_n\) become exactly \(0\); this low-dimensional case is handled as a direct consequence.

      ###### Statement
      Under the assumptions above, i.e. for fixed \(\delta\in(0,1/2)\) and under the conditions of Theorem~\ref{THM:G},
      \begin{equation}\label{IandIII}
      \I_n \ \lesssim \ n^{-\frac12+\delta}
      \qquad\text{and}\qquad
      \III_n \ \lesssim \ n^{-\frac12+\delta}.
      \end{equation}

Let \(m\ge1\). Let \(R\in\mathbb R^{m\times m}\) be a correlation matrix, and define \(R^+\) entrywise by
\[
R^+_{ij}=\max\{R_{ij},0\}.
\]
Suppose \(R^+\) is positive semidefinite, and suppose there exist constants \(\varepsilon_0\in(0,1)\) and \(C>0\), independent of \(m\), such that
\[
\max_{i\ne j}R_{ij}\le1-\varepsilon_0,
\qquad
\sum_{1\le i<j\le m}R^+_{ij}\le Cm.
\]
If \(\zeta\sim N(0,R)\), then there exists a constant \(C'>0\), independent of \(m\), such that
\[
\mathbb P\!\left(\max_{1\le j\le m}\zeta_j\le\sqrt{\log m}\right)
\le C'\exp\!\left(-\frac12 m^{1/3}\right).
\]

paper_939f6a24b4ee4e378c0de2ad4ed252f8.statement: Let $r,n\in\mathbb N$. Let $\mathcal C_r$ be the class of all Borel convex subsets of $\mathbb R^r$, and let $\gamma_r:=N(0,I_r)$ be the standard Gaussian probability measure on $\mathbb R^r$. For random vectors $X_1,\dots,X_n\in\mathbb R^r$, write $S_n^{(X)}:=\frac1{\sqrt n}\sum_{i=1}^n X_i$. Assume that $X_1,\dots,X_n$ are independent identically distributed Borel random vectors taking values in $\mathbb R^r$, with $\mathbb E[X_1]=0$, $\mathbb E[X_1X_1^\top]=I_r$, and $\mathbb E[\|X_1\|_2^3]<\infty$. No Gaussianity of $X_1$ is assumed. Then there exists an absolute constant $C>0$, independent of $r$, of $n$, and of the law of $X_1$, such that for every $r,n$ and every i.i.d. sequence $X_1,\dots,X_n$ satisfying the above assumptions, $\sup_{A\in\mathcal C_r}|\mathbb P((1/\sqrt n)\sum_{i=1}^n X_i\in A)-\gamma_r(A)|\le C\,r^{1/4}\,\mathbb E[\|X_1\|_2^3]\,n^{-1/2}$. Equivalently, $\sup_{A\in\mathcal C_r}|\mathbb P(S_n^{(X)}\in A)-\gamma_r(A)|\le C\,r^{1/4}\,\mathbb E[\|X_1\|_2^3]\,n^{-1/2}$. The bound is uniform over all Borel convex subsets of the ambient space $\mathbb R^r$.

In the specialization used in the selected proof, take $Y=\|Q^\top Z_1\|_2$, $r=3$, $s=4$. If $\mathbb E[\|Q^\top Z_1\|_2^4]<\infty$, then $\mathbb E[\|Q^\top Z_1\|_2^3]\le(\mathbb E[\|Q^\top Z_1\|_2^4])^{3/4}$. Since $\|Q^\top Z_1\|_2^2=Z_1^\top QQ^\top Z_1$, this is equivalently written as $\mathbb E[\|Q^\top Z_1\|_2^3]\le(\mathbb E[(Z_1^\top QQ^\top Z_1)^2])^{3/4}$. The inequality itself does not require independence, centering, standardization, Gaussianity, or positive definiteness. It requires only the stated finiteness of the higher moment.

Let \(r\ge1\), let \(m\ge1\) be an integer, and let \(\xi_1,\ldots,\xi_m\) be independent random variables satisfying \(\mathbb E[|\xi_j|^r]<\infty\) for all \(1\le j\le m\). There is an absolute constant \(c>0\), universal over \(r,m\) and over all such independent variables, such that:
1. If \(\xi_1,\ldots,\xi_m\) are nonnegative almost surely, then
\[\left\|\sum_{j=1}^m \xi_j\right\|_r\le c\,\frac{r}{\operatorname{Log}(r)}\max\left\{\left\|\sum_{j=1}^m \xi_j\right\|_1,\left(\sum_{j=1}^m \|\xi_j\|_r^r\right)^{1/r}\right\}.\]
2. If \(r>2\) and \(\mathbb E\xi_j=0\) for all \(1\le j\le m\), then
\[\left\|\sum_{j=1}^m \xi_j\right\|_r\le c\,\frac{r}{\operatorname{Log}(r)}\max\left\{\left\|\sum_{j=1}^m \xi_j\right\|_2,\left(\sum_{j=1}^m \|\xi_j\|_r^r\right)^{1/r}\right\}.\]

Let \(X\) be a real random variable. The following properties are equivalent; the positive parameters \(K_i>0\) appearing in these properties differ from each other by at most an absolute constant factor.
1. The tails of \(X\) satisfy \(\mathbb P\{|X|\ge t\}\le 2\exp(-t/K_1)\) for all \(t\ge0\).
2. The moments of \(X\) satisfy \(\|X\|_{L^p}=(\mathbb E|X|^p)^{1/p}\le K_2 p\) for all \(p\ge1\).
3. The moment-generating function of \(|X|\) satisfies \(\mathbb E\exp(\lambda|X|)\le \exp(K_3\lambda)\) for all \(\lambda\) such that \(0\le\lambda\le\frac1{K_3}\).
4. The moment-generating function of \(|X|\) is bounded at some positive point: \(\mathbb E\exp(|X|/K_4)\le 2\).
Moreover, if \(\mathbb E X=0\), then properties 1-4 are also equivalent to the following property.
5. The moment-generating function of \(X\) satisfies \(\mathbb E\exp(\lambda X)\le \exp(K_5^2\lambda^2)\) for all \(\lambda\) such that \(|\lambda|\le\frac1{K_5}\).
More precisely, there exists an absolute constant \(C\) such that property \(i\) implies property \(j\) with parameter \(K_j\le C K_i\), for any two properties \(i,j=1,2,3,4\).

Let \(X\) be a real random variable. The following properties are equivalent; the positive parameters \(K_i>0\) appearing in these properties differ from each other by at most an absolute constant factor.
1. The tails of \(X\) satisfy \(\mathbb P\{|X|\ge t\}\le 2\exp(-t/K_1)\) for all \(t\ge0\).
2. The moments of \(X\) satisfy \(\|X\|_{L^p}=(\mathbb E|X|^p)^{1/p}\le K_2 p\) for all \(p\ge1\).
3. The moment-generating function of \(|X|\) satisfies \(\mathbb E\exp(\lambda|X|)\le \exp(K_3\lambda)\) for all \(\lambda\) such that \(0\le\lambda\le\frac1{K_3}\).
4. The moment-generating function of \(|X|\) is bounded at some positive point: \(\mathbb E\exp(|X|/K_4)\le 2\).
Moreover, if \(\mathbb E X=0\), then properties 1-4 are also equivalent to the following property.
5. The moment-generating function of \(X\) satisfies \(\mathbb E\exp(\lambda X)\le \exp(K_5^2\lambda^2)\) for all \(\lambda\) such that \(|\lambda|\le\frac1{K_5}\).
More precisely, there exists an absolute constant \(C\) such that property \(i\) implies property \(j\) with parameter \(K_j\le C K_i\), for any two properties \(i,j=1,2,3,4\).

Assumption 2.1 gives \(\|Z_1^\top u\|_{\psi_1}\le c_0\) with \(c_0\) independent of \(n,p\). Applying the Vershynin sub-exponential moment bound yields \(\left\|\frac1{\sigma_j}(X_{1,j}-\mu_j)\right\|_q=\|Z_1^\top u\|_q\lesssim q\), the intermediate estimate used in the selected proof before applying Rosenthal's inequality.
